title: Sign, baby, sign!

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Throughout the world, many deaf people communicate through hand signals that are the words and phrases of the sign language used in the country in which they live. New research demonstrates that teaching such a sign language to babies who have no hearing problem improves their language skills as they develop. Dr Marilyn Daniels, a professor of speech communication at Pennsylvania State University and author of the book Dancing with Words: Signing for Hearing Children’s Literacy, is at the forefront of this research.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Dr Daniels is one of the few researchers working in this field who promotes teaching babies a national sign language instead of invented gestures or ‘home signs’. Since her work is in the United States, it is American Sign Language (ASL) that she prefers to teach babies with no hearing problems because ASL is a recognized language there. She says ‘In the United States, studying ASL is accepted as an alternative to studying a foreign language in high school in many states and in most colleges and universities. Why then would you not want to teach a hearing baby or child words that they could use later to help them in their academic pursuits? If you teach ASL signs, you are giving kids a huge advantage if they later choose to study ASL to fulfill foreign language study requirements.’

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Dr Daniels also notes that hearing children who are fluent in ASL will be able to communicate with deaf children and adults. But, most importantly, the fact that ASL is a real language is what makes it so beneficial to children’s development: ‘Because ASL is a legitimate language it is stored in a separate memory store in the baby’s or child’s brain. This happens even in the very first stages of learning the language.’ When hearing babies learn sign language, their brains develop further than those of babies who learn no second language. Dr Daniels explains: ‘Studies show that even when human beings are in the initial stages of acquiring a second language, their second language vocabulary is not stored in the same area of the left side of the brain as the person’s first language. This means that babies or children who have been presented with ASL or its vocabulary have an additional place for search and recall in their brains.’

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Learning ASL also furthers brain development in hearing babies, says Dr Daniels, because ‘ASL uses the eyes to a far greater degree than any spoken language. The eyes develop sooner in young children and when you take in information with your eyes you are using the right side of the brain.’ All languages are actually stored in the left side of the brain, but when babies learn sign language both the right side and the left side are used. ‘This is a wonderful advantage because you are using both hemispheres of the brain, building more synapses* in the brain,’ says Dr Daniels.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Sign language in general seems especially suitable for young children. ‘The motor areas of the body mature sooner than the mouth and other language articulators,’ says Dr Daniels. This means that it is easier for children to learn and remember signs than it is for them to acquire fluency in either spoken or written language. ‘Children like to use sign language,’ she adds. ‘They pay more attention because of the physical movement; they become more involved. They are involved and interested in the process of learning.’

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: For parents and teachers concerned with the education of hearing children, Dr Daniels’s research is most significant because it shows that using sign language from infancy until a child is 12 years old results in improved literacy. The children she has worked with demonstrate better recognition of letters and sounds, better spelling, and larger English-language vocabularies than children who were not taught sign language.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: For deaf people and the parents and teachers of deaf children, the interest in Dr Daniels’s research lies not only in the support it gives to sign language but also in its implications regarding the best way to educate deaf children. Many doctors, audiologists, and teachers of the deaf maintain that the best method for raising deaf children is to teach them to lip read and to try to make the sounds of language. Most cochlear implant** specialists maintain that the goal of implanting cochlear implants in babies and children — followed by years of intensive hearing and speaking therapy — is to help with language acquisition. ‘The idea that deaf children will not learn how to speak if they are taught sign language before they learn English or the language of their country is an outdated position,’ counters Dr Daniels. ‘I would totally disagree with this view.’

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: Dr Daniels’s research shows that deaf children’s comprehension of the spoken language can be improved if the indigenous sign language of the country is taught first. She says, ‘Deaf babies who are taught to speak still often have no language to use for thinking. All human beings need a language for communication with others, but they also need a language for thinking about things, for processing information. Speech and language are two very different things. Deaf babies must have a sign language; it is their natural language, and it should be established before they are taught the spoken and written language of their country.’

questions.prompt: Dr Daniels believes that parents should make up their own gestures to communicate with their babies.
American Sign Language is the most widely used sign language in the world.
For hearing children in America, learning American Sign Language is an equivalent option to learning a foreign language.
Brain research indicates that vocabulary is more easily learned than grammar.
First and second languages are stored on different sides of the brain.
Children have less difficulty learning to make signs than learning to make sounds.
According to Dr Daniels, the view that deaf children must learn lip reading before sign language is old fashioned.

subtitle: Hand signals used by the deaf are now used to communicate with babies who can hear
footnotes: ** cochlear implant: a small electronic device that can help to provide a sense of sound to a person who is profoundly deaf or severely hard of hearing
